title: Do Robust Intervals Help for a Difference in Means? Target Bias, the Side of Failure and a Two-Sample Expansion for Yuen’s Interval
content: Background: Robust intervals, such as Yuen’s trimmed-mean interval, the bootstrap-t on trimmed means, Huber M-estimation and empirical likelihood, are often recommended for small samples that are skewed or heavy-tailed. When the scientific target is the difference of arithmetic means δ = μ1 − μ2, the robust location estimators estimate a different quantity under skewness. We asked how these intervals fail when they are used for δ, on which side they fail, and whether a two-sample Edgeworth expansion for Yuen’s statistic predicts that side. Methods: A registered simulation study regenerated exactly the 147 settings and 10,000 datasets per setting of an earlier study: seven families, including t3, a contaminated normal and four lognormal designs with left and opposed skew; group sizes from 5 to 100; variance ratios 1, 4 and 10. The plan was frozen and deposited before any study computation. The arms were Welch’s interval, Yuen’s interval at 10% and 20% trimming, the bootstrap-t on trimmed means at both levels (1,999 resamples), a Huber M-interval (k = 1.345, fixed MAD scale) and empirical likelihood (exploratory). The outcomes were coverage, the probabilities L and U that the interval lies entirely below or entirely above the target, and L − U, for δ and for each method’s own target. Four hypotheses were tested; the predictions for the fourth were computed and dated before the plan was frozen. Results: Welch’s counts reproduced the archive exactly in all 147 settings. When the standardised target bias was large, Yuen’s 20% interval failed on the side opposite to the sign of the bias in 16 of 16 determined settings (10% trimming: 9 of 9; Huber: 13 of 13). Its directional error grew from (10,10) to (100,100) while Welch’s shrank, in all 8 determined series; with opposed skew and variance ratio 4, its coverage of δ fell from 0.77 at 5 per group to 0.002 at 100, while Welch’s rose from 0.85 to 0.93. With symmetric heavy tails, the trimmed intervals were narrower than Welch’s in 28 (Yuen) and 27 (bootstrap-t) of 42 settings, so this hypothesis was not supported; every failure had a group of 5, and the directional error was never larger than Welch’s. About Yuen’s own target, the predicted side was observed in 57 of 57 determined rows (Spearman 0.966; 10% trimming: 36 of 36, 0.915). The trimmed-mean intervals covered their own targets close to 0.95 in every family. The Huber interval under-covered even its own target, because the registered standard error ignores the estimated scale. Empirical likelihood under-covered in every family (exploratory). Conclusions: Used for δ, robust location intervals exchange the small-sample skewness error for a target bias that grows with the sample size. Their failure for δ is a failure of the estimand, not of calibration. With symmetric heavy tails, trimming shortened the interval without directional cost once both groups had at least 10 observations. A robust location interval answers a question about δ only when the populations are symmetric, or when the robust target is itself the quantity of interest and is reported as such.
